M5.about: Ravel’s earliest known piano work: a short, capricious serenade that alternates harsh, guitar-like ‘pizzicatissimo’ chords with mock-sentimental melody. Its bizarre twists show the influence of Emmanuel Chabrier, while its dissonant bite already points to the later Alborada del gracioso.
M5.ctx: Written as a teenager and never published in Ravel’s lifetime; he later mentioned it in his autobiographical sketch, naming Chabrier as its model. The autograph was rediscovered by the Ravel scholar Arbie Orenstein and first published in 1975, the centenary of Ravel’s birth.
facts: Ravel’s earliest known piano piece.
Unpublished until 1975.
Ravel named Chabrier as its model.
Henle rates it level 6.

M19.about: A slow, dignified dance evoking, in Ravel’s words, a pavane that a little princess might once have danced at the Spanish court. A simple, tender melody returns twice in a rondo-like form, each time more richly harmonised.
M19.ctx: Ravel said he chose the title mainly for its alliteration and warned against reading too much into it. The piece became enormously popular after its 1902 premiere, and Ravel himself orchestrated it in 1910 — though he later criticised the original for its too-obvious debt to Chabrier.
facts: Ravel chose the title for the sound of the words.
He orchestrated it himself in 1910.
Premiered by Ricardo Viñes, who gave many Ravel premieres.
Henle rates it level 6.

M30.about: A dazzling evocation of fountains and cascades in E major, built from shimmering arpeggios, glissando-like runs and bell-like chords. Its ‘floating’ harmony and new keyboard sonorities, heading the score with a line of verse by Henri de Régnier about a river god laughing at the water that tickles him, made it a landmark of modern piano writing.
M30.ctx: Written while Ravel was still a student of Fauré, to whom it is dedicated. Liszt had explored similar imagery in ‘Les jeux d’eaux à la Villa d’Este’. Ravel’s piece appeared before Debussy’s comparable water pieces and is often credited with pointing the way.
facts: Dedicated to his teacher Gabriel Fauré.
Headed by a line of verse by Henri de Régnier.
Henle rates it level 8 (ABRSM LRSM).

M40.about: A compact, classically proportioned sonatina in three movements, all built from the same falling-fourth motif. A graceful Modéré, a wistful minuet and a brilliant toccata-like finale show Ravel’s love of clarity and restraint.
M40.ctx: The first movement was probably written in 1903 for a competition run by a Parisian magazine; Ravel played it at a salon in January 1904 and added the other two movements later. Ravel valued the work highly and often included it in his own concerts, though he reportedly avoided the demanding finale.
parts: A graceful, flowing opening in miniature sonata form.
A brilliant, toccata-like finale that recalls earlier themes.
facts: The first movement began as a competition entry.
All three movements share one motif.
Henle rates the whole work level 7.

M43.about: Five ‘mirrors’, each dedicated to a member of the artists’ circle Les Apaches. From fluttering night moths and sad birds to a boat on the ocean, a Spanish ‘morning song of the jester’ and distant bells, the cycle pushed Ravel’s harmony further than ever before.
M43.ctx: Ravel said the music should sound as if it came from a sketchbook. Its bold harmonies first irritated contemporaries. He later orchestrated ‘Une barque sur l’océan’ and ‘Alborada del gracioso’; the Alborada in particular became one of his best-known works.
parts: Night moths: fluttering, chromatic figures, dedicated to Léon-Paul Fargue.
Sad birds lost in a dark forest, dedicated to Ricardo Viñes.
A boat on rolling waves of arpeggios, dedicated to Paul Sordes.
A virtuoso Spanish ‘morning song of the jester’, full of repeated notes and glissandi.
A valley of bells, calm and resonant, dedicated to Maurice Delage.
facts: Each piece is dedicated to a member of Les Apaches.
Ravel orchestrated Nos. 3 and 4.
Henle rates the pieces at levels 7–9.

M55.about: Three ‘poems for piano’ after prose poems by Aloysius Bertrand: the water nymph Ondine trying to seduce a mortal, a hanged man on a gibbet at sunset, and the malevolent goblin Scarbo. Ravel set out to write something harder than Balakirev’s ‘Islamey’, and Scarbo is widely regarded as one of the most difficult pieces in the repertoire.
M55.ctx: Written in 1908. Ravel called the work ‘three romantic poems of transcendental virtuosity’. Henle’s edition prints each of Bertrand’s poems before the piece it inspired.
parts: A water nymph’s seductive song over shimmering tremolos.
A hanged man at sunset, over an unbroken tolling B-flat.
A goblin darting in the night: fiendish repeated notes and sudden eruptions.
facts: Based on prose poems by Aloysius Bertrand.
Ravel wanted it to be harder than Balakirev’s ‘Islamey’.
Le Gibet sustains a single tolling B-flat throughout.
Henle rates the pieces at levels 8–9.

M72.about: Ravel’s ‘apotheosis of the Viennese waltz’: out of a murky haze, fragments of waltz tunes gradually take shape into a glittering ballroom, which then whirls into distortion and collapse. The solo version is a formidable piece of piano writing in its own right.
M72.ctx: Ravel had planned a waltz tribute to Johann Strauss since 1906. When Diaghilev commissioned a ballet in 1919 he returned to the idea, working simultaneously on the solo piano version, a two-piano version and the orchestral score. Diaghilev famously rejected it as ‘not a ballet, but the portrait of a ballet’.
facts: Ravel worked on the solo, two-piano and orchestral versions at the same time.
Diaghilev rejected it as a ballet.
Henle rates the solo version level 8.
